short: A direction that a square matrix only stretches: multiplying the eigenvector by the matrix gives the same vector times a number, the eigenvalue. In PCA the eigenvectors of the covariance or relationship matrix are the principal components.
long: For a square matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), a vector \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) with \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \ell\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector and \(\ell\) its eigenvalue. A symmetric matrix such as a covariance matrix or the genetic relationship matrix has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors, usually scaled to length 1. In genotype PCA, each eigenvector of the \(n \times n\) relationship matrix holds one score per person: PLINK writes them, one column per component, to its .eigenvec file. The sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary (\(-\mathbf{v}\) is also an eigenvector), so the same analysis run twice can mirror a PC plot.
l1: Slides 102–103 and the PCA sections of page 7; PLINK's .eigenvec file in QC step 6.

short: The number by which a square matrix stretches one of its eigenvectors. In PCA it is the variance of the data along that principal component, so an eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues is the component's share of the variance.
long:
If \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \ell\mathbf{v}\), then \(\ell\) is the eigenvalue of the eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\). The eigenvalues of a covariance matrix are non-negative and add up to its trace, the total variance. For the genetic relationship matrix of \(n\) people the trace is close to \(n\), so a component's share of the genotype variance is about \(\ell_k/n\). PLINK writes the top eigenvalues to its .eigenval file; dividing one of them by the sum of only those reported overstates its share.

Worked example (page 7): a relationship matrix of six people has eigenvalues 5.173, 1.184, 0.800, 0.408, 0 and 0; their sum, 7.566, is the trace, so PC1 captures 68.4% of the variance.
l1: Slides 102–103; PLINK's .eigenval file in QC step 6; scree plots for choosing the number of PCs.

links.t: Patterson et al. 2006, Population structure and eigenanalysis

short: In STRUCTURE-type models, the fraction of a person's allele copies that the model assigns to each of K fitted ancestral components. A person's K proportions are non-negative and add up to 1; they depend on K and on which people are analyzed.
long:
The model draws each allele copy of person \(i\) from component \(k\) with probability \(q_{ik}\), so the genotype at SNP \(j\) is \(\Binomial(2, \sum_k q_{ik} f_{kj})\), where \(f_{kj}\) is the component's allele frequency. ADMIXTURE writes the estimates to its .Q file (one row per person, one column per component), and bar plots draw each row as one stacked bar.

A proportion is a property of the fit, not of the person's family tree: with a different \(K\), different reference samples or a population missing from the sample, the same person gets different proportions (Lawson et al. 2018).
l1: Slides 99–101; the bar plots of slide 100; the ADMIXTURE widget on page 7.

links.t: Lawson, van Dorp & Falush 2018, how not to over-interpret STRUCTURE and ADMIXTURE bar plots

short: The simplest model of genetic drift: each generation has N people (2N allele copies), and every copy of the next generation is drawn at random from the copies of the current one, so the next allele count is binomial with 2N trials.
long: With frequency \(p_t\) in generation \(t\), the next count is \(\Binomial(2N, p_t)\): the frequency keeps its mean and changes by a random amount with variance \(p_t(1 - p_t)/(2N)\). Populations that split from one ancestor drift apart, with \(\Var(p_t) = p_0(1 - p_0)F_t\) and \(F_t = 1 - (1 - 1/2N)^t\). Generations do not overlap and there is no selection, mutation or migration; real populations are described by the effective population size, the \(N\) of a Wright–Fisher population that drifts at the same rate.
l1: Slide 97 (drift); the drift widget on page 7.

links.t: Coop, Population and quantitative genetics notes

short: Wright's model of migration: many populations of N people each receive, every generation, a fraction m of their parents from a common pool. Drift and migration balance at an F_ST of about 1/(1 + 4Nm).
long: Two copies sampled from one population share an ancestral copy with probability \(F_{t+1} = 1/(2N) + (1 - 1/2N)(1 - m)^2 F_t\), which levels off at \(F^{*} \approx 1/(1 + 4Nm)\). Only the number of migrants per generation, \(Nm\), matters: one migrant per generation holds \(F_{\mathrm{ST}}\) near 0.2 whatever the population size. When migrants come mainly from neighbors (isolation by distance), the same balance produces clines.
l1: Slides 89–91 and 97 (migration); the drift widget on page 7 has a migration slider.

short: A square table with the covariance of every pair of variables; the diagonal holds the variances. For a data matrix whose columns are centered, it is the transpose of the matrix times the matrix, divided by the number of rows minus 1.
long: For centered data \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(n\) rows, \(d\) columns), \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}/(n - 1)\) is \(d \times d\). PCA is its eigendecomposition: the eigenvectors are the directions of the principal components and the eigenvalues their variances. Genotype PCA usually works with the \(n \times n\) person-by-person matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}/m\) instead (the genetic relationship matrix), which gives the same components through the singular value decomposition.
l1: Slide 102 (PCA in general); page 7, PCA in general.

links.t: Jolliffe & Cadima 2016, Principal component analysis: a review

short: The factorization of any matrix into an orthonormal matrix, a diagonal matrix of non-negative singular values and another orthonormal matrix. For a genotype matrix it gives the person scores and the SNP weights of PCA at once.
long: \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\): the columns of \(\mathbf{U}\) (people) are the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\), the columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) (SNPs) the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}\), and the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}/m\) are \(s_k^2/m\). Large-sample PCA software (PLINK 2's approx mode, FlashPCA2, bigsnpr) computes the top singular vectors directly with randomized or iterative algorithms.
l1: Page 7, the same components from the people-by-people matrix.

short: How much one SNP contributes to a principal component: the SNP's entry in the component's direction vector. A person's score is the weighted sum of their standardized genotypes, so the weights are what projection uses.
long: In \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\), column \(k\) of \(\mathbf{V}\) holds the SNP weights of component \(k\). Plotting them along the genome shows what a component captures: weights spread over the whole genome indicate population structure, weights concentrated in one region indicate a region of long-range LD. PLINK 1.9 writes them with --pca var-wts, PLINK 2 with --pca allele-wts.
l1: Page 7, the worked PCA example and projection.

short: Placing new people on principal components computed from other people (for example a reference panel) by multiplying their standardized genotypes by the SNP weights. The axes then do not depend on the new people, but projected scores shrink toward the origin.
long: For a new person with standardized genotypes \(z_j\) (standardized with the reference allele frequencies), the coordinate on component \(k\) is \(\sum_j z_j v_{jk}/\sqrt{m}\), on the scale of \(\mathbf{u}_k\sqrt{\ell_k}\). Because the weights were fitted to the reference people, new people sit closer to the origin than reference people from the same population (shrinkage), more so on later components (Privé et al. 2020). PLINK 1.9 projects with --pca-cluster-names; PLINK 2 with --pca allele-wts followed by --score.

links.t: Privé et al. 2020, best practices for PCA of population genetic data

short: A plot of the eigenvalues of a PCA in decreasing order. Components that reflect real structure stand above a smooth floor of small eigenvalues produced by noise; the bend where the floor starts suggests how many components to keep.
long: For genotype data, plot \(\ell_k\) (or \(\ell_k\) divided by the trace) against \(k\). The floor is not flat: random genotypes also give a decreasing sequence of eigenvalues, so a formal test (Tracy–Widom) or a look at what each component separates is used alongside the plot.
l1: Page 7, how many PCs; the PCA widget shows the top 8 eigenvalues as a bar chart.

short: A test of whether the largest remaining eigenvalue of a genotype PCA is larger than expected if there were no population structure, using the Tracy–Widom distribution of the largest eigenvalue of a random matrix.
long: Patterson, Price and Reich (2006) introduced it for genotype data; EIGENSOFT's twstats program applies it to each eigenvalue in turn. In large samples it declares many components significant, including components produced by long-range LD or by relatives, so significance alone does not say that a component reflects ancestry.

short: A simulation method for Bayesian models: it produces a long sequence of parameter values in which each value depends on the previous one and values appear in proportion to their posterior probability, so averages over the sequence estimate the parameters and their uncertainty.
long: STRUCTURE (Pritchard et al. 2000) uses MCMC to sample admixture proportions and component allele frequencies from their posterior distribution, which takes much longer than ADMIXTURE's maximum-likelihood fit but gives a spread of plausible values. The first part of the sequence (burn-in) is discarded because it still depends on the starting values.

short: Judging a model by how well it predicts data it was not fitted to: split the data into parts (folds), fit on all but one part, predict the held-out part, and repeat for each part. The average prediction error compares models, for example different numbers of components K.
long: ADMIXTURE's --cv option (5 folds by default) hides a fifth of the observed genotypes at a time, refits the model and predicts each hidden genotype from \(2\sum_k q_{ik}f_{kj}\); the screen output reports "CV error (K=…)". A lower error suggests a better \(K\), but in human data, where populations are connected by migration and clines, there is usually no single true \(K\).

links.t: Alexander & Lange 2011, Enhancements to the ADMIXTURE algorithm

aka: time to the most recent common ancestor
short: For two allele copies, the number of generations back to their most recent common ancestor copy. Copies from the same population usually coalesce more recently than copies from different populations.
long: In a Wright–Fisher population of \(N\) people two copies coalesce with probability \(1/(2N)\) per generation, so their expected coalescence time is \(2N\) generations. McVean (2009) showed that the expected entries of the genetic relationship matrix, and therefore the PCs, are determined by the average coalescence times between pairs of people relative to the sample average, which is why the positions on a PC plot depend on how many people from each population are sampled.

links.t: McVean 2009, A genealogical interpretation of PCA

short: A variant whose minor allele is seen exactly once in a sample: one copy in one person. Large sequencing samples contain many singletons, because most variants arose recently and are rare.
long: In a population of constant size the expected number of variant sites whose derived allele appears in \(i\) of the \(2n\) sampled copies is proportional to \(1/i\), so singletons are the most common class. Human samples have even more, because the population grew rapidly in recent history (Keinan & Clark 2012). Whether a variant is a singleton depends on the sample: it may be common elsewhere.

links.t: Keinan & Clark 2012, excess of rare variants
